isOpenEnded: While more information would be helpful in coming to a decision, in the abstract it seems fair that Claimant should bear a greater than 50% responsibility for fees of the Centre and the tribunal.  Claimant brought proceedings on a claim that was ultimately found not to have been established, and in so doing inflicted financial costs of Respondent.  On the other hand, both parties benefited from the availability of the process to resolve their disputes (one perhaps more directly than the other), and it seems likely that Claimant may have prevailed on at least some issues, such as jurisdiction.  Thus, it may not be equitable to require Claimant to pay all of these costs.  With respect to counsel fees, these are typically much greater than those of the arbitrators.  At first blush, one might conclude that, because these represent a much higher cost to Respondent as a result of the unsuccessful proceedings than do the Centre's and arbitrator's fees, the reasoning above would, a fortiori, require Claimant to pay all or at least part of them.  On the other hand, there are much greater uncertainties with respect to counsel fees, including reasonableness of the basis for the charges, reasonableness of the work done, the extent to which the parties were successful on particular issues, etc.  In addition, the potential risk of having to pay the other side's very large counsel fees may have a very strong chilling effect on Claimants who have good arguable claims, but cannot afford to undertake such a high exposure in order to present them - particularly as the investor-state dispute resolutino process entails a fairly high degree of uncertainty.  In light of these factors, I would be reluctant to require one side to reimburse the other's legal fees in a case where the first party was "merely" unsuccessful as to the merits of its claims.
